Terraria.verdict: A 2D sandbox where you dig, build and fight bosses, sold for a one-time $4.99 with no ads or in-app purchases.
Terraria.bestFor: Players who like open-ended building and exploring and want a big game without any extra spending.
pros: One-time $4.99 price with no ads and no IAP
Huge mix of digging, crafting, building and boss fights
Rated 4.6★ by players
Works well for long play sessions
cons: Touch controls take time to get used to
Little guidance at the start, so new players may feel lost
body: You start with a few basic tools in a randomly made 2D world. You chop trees, dig underground, collect ores and craft better gear. Along the way you build houses that attract townspeople and take on enemies and bosses.
The game does not tell you much, so the first hour is about trying things and learning what works. Once you find caves, dungeons and new biomes, goals appear on their own.
It suits patient players who like to set their own goals. Because there are no ads or purchases, you pay once and get the full game.
Terraria.author: editors

Match-Factory.verdict: A relaxing match-3 puzzle where you pick items off shelves and group three of the same kind to clear them.
Match-Factory.bestFor: Casual players who want quick, calm puzzle levels with no ads.
pros: No ads, which is rare for a free puzzle game
Rated 4.7★ with over 10 million installs
Easy to learn and suits short sessions
Suitable for all ages
cons: Later levels can push you toward buying boosters
Gameplay stays much the same from level to level
body: Each level gives you a shelf full of small items, such as toys and snacks. You tap three matching ones to send them to your tray and clear them. The tray has limited room, so you have to plan which items to pick first.
Levels are short and get harder as more item types and tricky layouts appear. Boosters can help when you get stuck.
The game is free and has no ads, but it does sell in-app purchases. It fits anyone who wants a quiet puzzle to play for a few minutes at a time.
Match-Factory.author: editors

Muse-Dash.verdict: A rhythm game where your character runs along while you tap to hit enemies and dodge obstacles in time with the music.
Muse-Dash.bestFor: Rhythm fans who like cute art and a soundtrack of Japanese-style pop and electronic songs.
pros: Simple two-lane tap controls that are easy to pick up
Colorful anime-style art
No ads and a low $2.99 price
Several difficulty levels for each song
cons: Extra song packs are sold through in-app purchases
Hard difficulties are tough for beginners
body: Notes and enemies come at you on two lanes, and you tap or hold buttons on the beat. Some enemies are on the ground and some are in the air, so you have to switch quickly. Missing hits drains your health.
Each song has several difficulty levels, so you can start easy and work up. Its cute characters and bright stages make the game look lighter than it plays.
The base game costs $2.99 and has no ads. It suits music fans who like to replay songs and improve their scores.
Muse-Dash.author: editors

Stumble-Guys.verdict: A party-style online race where you run, jump and wobble through obstacle courses against other players.
Stumble-Guys.bestFor: Friends and casual players who want fast, silly online matches.
pros: Free to play with simple controls
Matches are short and easy to jump into
Lots of different maps and costumes
Rated 4.7★ with over 100 million installs
cons: In-app purchases for cosmetics and passes
Results often feel random, which can be annoying
body: You race with a big group of players through obstacle courses full of spinning bars, slippery slopes and moving platforms. Only the fastest finishers move on to the next round, and the last one standing wins the crown.
Controls are just a joystick and a jump button, so anyone can start playing right away. Matches are short, which makes it good for a quick game.
The game is free, with ads and optional purchases that mostly cover looks. It fits players who want light competition and don't mind some chaos.
Stumble-Guys.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.verdict: A survival horror game where you watch cameras and fix systems to stay alive against one haunting animatronic.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.bestFor: Horror fans who like tense, short nights and are fine with jump scares.
pros: One $2.99 price with no ads or IAP
Different mechanics from the first two games
Very tense atmosphere
cons: Jump scares are not for everyone
Short game that can feel repetitive after you learn it
body: You play a night guard in a haunted attraction. You flip through security cameras, play audio lures and reboot broken systems like ventilation and audio while one animatronic stalks you.
Each night is only a few minutes, but you have to keep an eye on several things at once. Learning how the enemy moves is the key to getting through.
It suits players who enjoy horror and don't mind dying a lot. The price is low and nothing else is for sale.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-3.author: editors

Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.verdict: A horror game set in a child's bedroom where you listen at doors and watch for animatronics creeping closer.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.bestFor: Players who like scary games that depend on careful listening.
pros: No ads and no IAP for $2.99
Sound plays a big part, so headphones help
Different setup from earlier games, with no cameras
cons: Jump scares are frequent and loud
body: You are in a dark bedroom with doors, a closet and a hallway. You close doors and listen for breathing to tell if an animatronic is near. Using the flashlight at the wrong moment can get you caught.
Nights are short, but they demand good timing and attention to sound. Wearing headphones makes the game easier and scarier.
It is best for fans of the series or for horror players who want a tough challenge. You pay once and there are no extras to buy.
Five-Nights-at-Freddys-4.author: editors

Friday-Night-Funkin.verdict: A rhythm game where you press arrow notes in time to beat rap opponents, with a lively cartoon style.
Friday-Night-Funkin.bestFor: Music game fans who want a free, stylish game with catchy songs.
pros: Free with no IAP
Catchy original songs and bold cartoon art
Rated 4.8★ by players
Easy to learn with arrow-based controls
body: You play a boy who battles opponents in rap duels. Arrows scroll up the screen, and you tap matching arrows in time with the song. Hitting notes well builds your score and keeps your health up.
The weeks of songs ramp up in difficulty, and each has its own characters and style. Missing too many notes makes you lose, so you often replay songs.
The game is free and has no in-app purchases, though ads appear. It suits players who like rhythm games and want something with personality.
Friday-Night-Funkin.author: editors

WorldBox.verdict: A sandbox god game where you create a world, add creatures and watch their civilizations grow or collapse.
WorldBox.bestFor: Creative players who like experimenting and watching what happens.
pros: Free to start
Lots of tools for terrain, animals and disasters
Open-ended, with no fixed goals
Suitable for all ages
cons: Little structure for players who want goals
body: You begin with an empty map and use god powers to shape land, plant forests and add humans, elves, orcs and dwarves. Then you watch them build villages, trade and go to war.
You can also trigger disasters like meteors, lightning and acid rain. Much of the fun is seeing how your choices play out.
It suits players who like to tinker and don't need missions. The base game is free, but ads and some paid features are part of it.
WorldBox.author: editors

Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.verdict: A simple puzzle where you pour colored water between tubes until each tube holds one color.
Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.bestFor: Players who want an easy, quiet puzzle to play in short breaks.
pros: Easy rules with no time limit
Free and suitable for all ages
Rated 4.8★ with over 10 million installs
cons: Purchases can remove ads or add extras
Levels can feel samey over time
body: You tap a tube and pour its top color into another tube with the same color on top. The goal is to sort every tube so it holds only one color. You have limited space, so mistakes can leave you stuck.
There is no timer, so you can think at your own pace. You can undo moves or add an empty tube if you get stuck.
It fits people who like calm logic puzzles. Expect ads, though, as the game is free.
Water-Sort-Puz---Color-Game.author: editors

Papas-Cupcakeria-To-Go.verdict: A time-management game where you take orders, bake and decorate cupcakes for customers.
Papas-Cupcakeria-To-Go.bestFor: Fans of cooking and time-management games who want a one-time purchase.
pros: No ads
Fun mix of baking, decorating and serving
$1.99 one-time price
Suitable for all ages
cons: Repeating the same tasks can get dull
Fewer installs and a lower 4.4★ than similar games
body: You run a cupcake shop. You take orders, bake the cupcakes, add frosting and toppings, and serve customers before they lose patience. Better results earn more tips.
As days pass you unlock new ingredients and upgrades for the shop. Orders get more complex, so you need to work faster and stay organized.
It suits players who like cooking games and light time pressure. There are no ads, which makes it easy to play in short bursts.
Papas-Cupcakeria-To-Go.author: editors

Papas-Cheeseria-To-Go.verdict: A restaurant management game where you build, grill and serve sandwiches to a growing line of customers.
Papas-Cheeseria-To-Go.bestFor: Players who enjoy cooking games and want a no-ads purchase.
pros: No ads
Rated 4.6★
Varied stations from building sandwiches to grilling and cooking
Priced at $1.99
body: You take customers' orders, then build sandwiches and cook them on a grill. You add toppings and finish each plate to match the order. Faster, more accurate service earns bigger tips.
New ingredients and upgrades unlock as you earn money and get new customers. The tasks stay similar, but the orders get more demanding.
It fits fans of the Papa's series and anyone who likes light time-management. Its $1.99 price and lack of ads make it easy to try.
Papas-Cheeseria-To-Go.author: editors

Bad-Piggies.verdict: A physics puzzle where you build odd vehicles from parts to carry a pig to the finish line.
Bad-Piggies.bestFor: Players who like to tinker and test ideas in a lighthearted puzzle game.
pros: Free with creative vehicle building
Familiar characters from Angry Birds
Suitable for all ages
cons: Lowest rating of this group at 4.2★
body: Each level gives you a few parts such as wheels, engines and fans. You build a vehicle and send the pig to a goal. Some levels also ask you to collect stars or finish in time.
There is more than one solution to most levels. Trial and error is the heart of it, and watching your machine fail is part of the fun.
It suits players who like physics and building. Expect ads, and some paid options if you want to move faster.
Bad-Piggies.author: editors

lists.title: Best horror games for a dark room
intro: These are scary games you pay for once and then play with no ads and no in-app shop. Nothing interrupts the tension, and nothing asks you for more money halfway through.
All of them are rated Teen. Play them with headphones on and the lights low, and skip them if jump scares aren't your thing.

picks.why: You watch cameras and vents from one office to keep a single animatronic away, for $2.99.
You sit in a dark bedroom and listen at doors for footsteps and breathing, which makes sound the main clue.
Sister Location gives you different tasks on each night instead of one repeated office job.
You explore an abandoned toy factory, solve puzzles with a grabbing hand tool and get chased, for $2.99.
This second chapter picks up the factory story with new areas and puzzles, though its 4.0 rating is lower than chapter 1.
Chapter 4 takes the story deeper into the factory at $4.99, and it suits players who finished the earlier chapters.
Bendy: Lone Wolf is a survival game set in the ink-stained studio, and its 4.5 rating is among the best here.

lists.howWeChose: We picked paid horror games with no ads and no in-app purchases, then favoured those with Google Play ratings of 4.0 or higher.
lists.author: editors

Most are free with ads, so they suit short sessions on the bus or at home.

picks.why: You hit notes on two lanes while your character runs, and the game costs $2.99 with no ads.
You press arrows in time to music to win singing duels, and it has no in-app purchases.
You tap falling tiles in time to well-known piano songs, and millions of people play it.
You tap along to piano pieces with a gentle difficulty curve, and it's free with ads.
You drag sounds onto characters to build your own music loop, and it's rated Everyone.
This beat-making game has no in-app purchases, though it is rated Teen.

lists.howWeChose: We looked for games where timing or sound is the main idea and kept ones rated 4.3 or higher on Google Play.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best sandbox and builder games for slow evenings
intro: These games give you a blank space and let you decide what to do with it. You can dig, plan a city, run a farm or shape a whole world.
There are no timers to beat. Pick one, put on a podcast and play at your own speed.

picks.why: You dig, build and fight through a 2D world for $4.99, with no ads and no in-app purchases.
You shape land, spawn creatures and watch their villages grow, or cause disasters if you want to.
You lay out roads, zones and services to grow a pixel-art city, and it has a 4.7 rating.
You build and run a theme park-style world with no ads, though it does have in-app purchases.
You draw subway lines to move passengers around a growing city, for $0.99 with no ads.
You drive tractors and harvesters to grow and sell crops, for $5.99.

lists.howWeChose: We picked games with open-ended play and no strict time limits, and kept those rated 4.3 or higher on Google Play.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best satisfying sorting and matching games
intro: Sorting and matching games have simple goals, such as getting every colour in the right place or clearing a pile of tiles. They suit tired evenings.
Each one below is rated Everyone, and most have a rating of 4.5 or higher.

picks.why: You match three identical items to clear them, and the game has no ads.
You pour coloured water between tubes until each tube holds one colour.
You sort coloured nuts onto bolts, and it has a 4.9 rating on Google Play.
You collect sets of three matching tiles, and over 100 million people have installed it.
You move buses out of a traffic jam so passengers can get on.
This is a wood-themed block puzzle with a 4.9 rating.

lists.howWeChose: We chose puzzles about sorting or matching, kept them rated Everyone, and favoured those with strong Google Play ratings.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best cooking and restaurant games
intro: In these games you take orders, prepare food and serve customers before they lose patience. They suit people who like a steady rhythm.
The Papa's games are paid, while the rest are free with ads.

picks.why: You take orders, bake cupcakes and add frosting and toppings, for $1.99 with no ads.
You grill sandwiches to order and add toppings, and it has a 4.6 rating.
You prepare coffee drinks and treats for customers, for $1.99 with no ads.
You serve customers quickly as they arrive, and it has a 4.7 rating.
You cook dishes for restaurant guests and the game is free with ads.
You make pizzas with toppings of your choice, and it's rated Everyone.

lists.howWeChose: We picked games where cooking and serving customers is the main task, and we mixed paid and free options so every budget has a choice.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best physics games for tinkerers
intro: These games make you test ideas and watch what happens. You might build a vehicle, guide water or push a wobbly character around.
Failing is part of it, and a lot of the fun comes from the odd things that happen when a plan goes wrong.

picks.why: You build odd vehicles from crates and wheels to get a pig to the finish.
You dig through dirt to guide water to Swampy's shower, and it costs $1.99.
You guide water through levels with more bright new ideas, and the game is free with ads.
You design bridges that vehicles must cross, for $2.99 with no ads or purchases.
You steer a floppy character through puzzles by grabbing, pushing and climbing.
You drive uphill over bumps and balance your car while managing fuel.

lists.howWeChose: We picked games whose main challenge comes from how objects move and fall, and kept those rated 3.8 or higher on Google Play.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best one-thumb games for the bus or train
intro: You can play these with one hand while holding a rail or a bag. The controls are tapping, holding or swiping.
Runs are short, so you can stop when your stop arrives.

picks.why: You swipe to dodge trains and collect coins, and over a billion people have installed it.
You hold the screen to fly your jetpack through a lab while dodging lasers.
You tap to swing a stickman from hook to hook, with one-touch controls.
You tap to jump a block over spikes in time to music, for $3.99 with no ads.
You hold to flip while sandboarding down dunes, and the pace is calm.
You swipe to slide your mask through maze tunnels, and each swipe moves you until you hit a wall.

lists.howWeChose: We kept games that can be played with one thumb and have simple, quick levels, then favoured those with 4.2 or higher on Google Play.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best pet-care games for young animal fans
intro: Children who like animals can feed, wash and play with a virtual pet in these games. They have no fighting and are all rated Everyone.
All of them are free with ads and in-app purchases, so a parent may want to switch off purchases in Google Play.

picks.why: You feed, bathe and play with Tom, and he repeats what you say in a funny voice.
You look after Tom and five friends who share one house, and it has over 500 million installs.
You help Hank play and look after tropical islands, with a 4.2 rating.
You feed, wash and play with an alien pet, and the game has over a billion installs.
You look after a virtual pet, and the game has no in-app purchases.
You play with a cute cat in a restaurant setting, and it's rated Everyone.

lists.howWeChose: We picked pet-care games rated Everyone with no violence, and checked ad and purchase details so parents know what to expect.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best sports games that aren't football
intro: Football gets most of the attention, but phones are also good for pool, darts, golf and other sports. These games suit a casual player.
You can try most of them for free.

picks.why: You aim and shoot to pot balls against real players, and it has a 4.8 rating.
You flick darts at the board in quick matches, and it's rated Everyone.
You play real-style golf rounds online or solo, with a 4.0 rating.
You pull back and release arrows at targets, and over 50 million people have installed it.
You time flips off a diving board to land cleanly, with a 4.5 rating.
This is a '90s kids' baseball game for $4.99 with no ads and no in-app purchases.

lists.howWeChose: We kept sports titles that have nothing to do with football, and chose those that are easy to learn.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best board-game classics on your phone
intro: These are digital versions of games many people already know, including chess, Monopoly and UNO. You can play against others online or on one phone.
The paid ones have no ads.

picks.why: You play chess against people online and use the built-in lessons to improve.
You play the familiar colour-and-number card game against others, and it's rated Everyone.
You buy properties and trade with rivals, for $4.99 with no ads.
You spin the wheel and pick life choices, for $4.99 with no ads.
You roll dice to move around boards and collect rewards, and it has no ads.
You play Scrabble-style word duels against friends or strangers.
Everyone gets the same place except one spy, and you pass one phone around the group.

lists.howWeChose: We chose well-known tabletop games with working digital versions, then checked ads and prices so the pick suits both groups and solo players.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best last-one-standing games
intro: In these games many players start in one arena and only one person, or one team, finishes. The matches are short, so you can fit one into a gap.
Silly party games and serious shooters are both on this list.

picks.why: Dozens of players race through obstacle courses, and each round eliminates some of them.
You pick a brawler and fight in Showdown matches, and the game has no ads.
You drop onto an island with other players and survive until you are the last one standing.
You play a large battle royale with vehicles and squads, and it's rated Teen.
You place bombs to blast rivals in a small arena, with a 4.4 rating.
You play cartoon mini-games and bomb brawls with friends on one device.

lists.howWeChose: We picked games built around elimination, from silly obstacle courses to proper battle royale, and checked each for a rating of 4.2 or higher.
lists.author: editors

lists.title: Best base-building games for daily check-ins
intro: These games ask you to log in, collect resources, upgrade buildings and train troops, a little at a time. A few minutes a day is enough to make progress.
All are free with no ads, but they have in-app purchases and long timers, so expect to wait.

picks.why: You build a village, train troops and raid other players, and it's rated Everyone 10+.
You build a base and army in a world hit by zombies, with over 100 million installs.
You grow a castle, train troops and join an alliance, and it's rated Everyone 10+.
You build a kingdom and fight with dragons, with an alliance-driven focus.
You rescue survivors and build a base while taking on zombies, with a 4.5 rating.

lists.howWeChose: We picked free base-building games with no ads and good Google Play ratings, and we tell you upfront that they run on timers.

method: {site} helps you decide which Android games are worth your time, money and storage space. We look at how a game starts, how quickly it becomes fun, how fair it feels over time and how it treats your attention and wallet.

Each game is scored out of 5 on four things: how good it is to play, how easy it is to learn, how well it runs on an ordinary phone and how fair its ads and purchases are. Games with a clear rating on Google Play and a score of 4 or more can be considered for Editor's Choice, which marks the games we'd suggest first in a list.

Ratings, install counts, prices, and information about ads and in-app purchases come from Google Play and refresh daily. If a developer changes a price or adds ads, the page will usually reflect that within a day. Our written comments are our own.
The games are made by their developers and are downloaded from Google Play. {site} does not make them and is not affiliated with Google or any game publisher.
Publishers cannot pay to be on a list or to move up. A game gets a place only because it fits the list and has a good record.
We revisit our lists regularly, and we update them sooner when a game changes its price, adds ads or gets a big update. If a game stops being a good fit, we take it out.

spotlight.why: Two-lane rhythm play with cute characters.
Silly obstacle races, free, suits any age.
